The central question is: when a transformer processes a long in-context learning (ICL) prompt with many demonstrations, how do earlier-layer residual stream representations get progressively distorted or overwritten by feature directions that encode "this is an ICL context" rather than task-specific content — and does this saturation degrade the model's ability to generalize from those demonstrations? The residual stream is not a neutral carrier; each layer adds its update directly via addition, so if attention heads in layers 4–8 are strongly writing a "demonstration boundary" or "pattern-match mode" feature direction, that vector persists and compounds into later layers unless something actively suppresses it. Cross-layer suppression is the underappreciated mechanism: later MLP layers or attention heads can in principle read that saturated direction and write a corrective negative projection, but this is not guaranteed and may consume representational capacity that would otherwise serve the actual task. The key concepts to hold simultaneously are: residual stream as a shared communication bandwidth, feature superposition (many features packed into the same high-dimensional space), and the distinction between a feature being suppressed (actively canceled by a later component) versus merely diluted (crowded out as more tokens are processed).

What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is the asymmetry of write costs: early layers pay no explicit penalty for polluting the residual stream with ICL-bookkeeping features, but late layers — where task-relevant computations like next-token prediction actually crystallize — inherit that pollution and may not have the capacity to fully clean it up, leading to systematic errors that look like "the model forgot the pattern" but are actually a geometry problem in activation space.

For a late-layer MLP to actively suppress a saturation feature f, its input weight matrix W_in must have a row (a neuron's input direction) with high cosine similarity to f — the neuron has to read the feature — and then the corresponding output weight (that neuron's column in W_out) must point in a direction that opposes f in the residual stream, i.e., W_out[:,k] ≈ −λf for some positive λ. This is the "read-then-write-negative" signature: without the read step, the MLP simply cannot act on the feature regardless of what W_out looks like. Anthropic's superposition work (Elhage et al., 2022) and the follow-on monosemanticity paper (Bricken et al., 2023) establish that neurons are often not feature-aligned — features are distributed across neurons — so in practice you'd look for this suppression pattern in the sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature basis, not the neuron basis: a SAE latent active on f whose downstream effect (via the decoder direction re-entering the residual stream) is a negative projection onto f's own direction. To distinguish active suppression from mere non-reading, the operational test is a causal intervention: patch f into the residual stream at the MLP's input and measure whether the MLP's output reduces the norm of f in the stream (suppression) versus leaves it unchanged (non-reading); Hernandez et al.'s ROME-style factual association work (2023) gives a template for exactly this kind of layer-wise causal tracing. A subtler diagnostic uses the MLP's Jacobian evaluated at typical ICL-saturated activations: if ∂(MLP output)/∂f has a large negative component along f, suppression is active; if the Jacobian is near-zero in that direction, the feature is invisible to that MLP regardless of what it theoretically could write. The expert worry here is that these two cases — suppression and non-reading — can produce identical residual stream outputs at any single forward pass, so you cannot distinguish them without either weight-level analysis or the patching intervention; behavioral experiments alone are blind to the difference.

The analogy is to the "distributed representations of context" finding in Hernandez et al. (2023) on factual recall, where causal tracing showed that no single MLP owned a fact; when suppression looks like that, it suggests the training signal was "predict well given ICL demonstrations," and feature reduction was a byproduct of the model learning to weight task-relevant directions more heavily — not a dedicated circuit. A concrete discriminating test: if you ablate suppression across layers cumulatively (zero out MLP k's contribution, then k and k+1, etc.) and the saturation feature f recovers smoothly and proportionally, the suppression is redundant/distributed-emergent; if it recovers in a step-function at one layer, a dedicated circuit exists there. Conmy et al.'s circuit-finding work (ACDC, 2023) operationalizes exactly this kind of structured ablation, and the smoothness-vs-step-function signature is a direct interpretable output of that method. The deeper implication is about credit assignment during training: if suppression is distributed, no individual weight update "knew" it was building a suppression mechanism — each update reduced loss marginally, and the suppression pattern is only visible post-hoc as a collective property, which means it is also fragile to fine-tuning in unpredictable ways, since no single component "owns" the behavior.

A further shortcut exploits attention pattern sparsity: at each layer, compute the attention weights from non-delimiter positions to delimiter positions; L* is approximately the earliest layer where this cross-position attention weight, multiplied by the f-norm at delimiter positions, exceeds a threshold in expectation — this is a purely forward-pass observable requiring no patching at all, though it conflates attention weight with causal influence in the way Jain & Wallace warned against. The expert caveat is that L* is not a single fixed layer but a distribution over heads: some heads at layer 6 may spread f while others at layer 6 do not, so the practically useful object is not one threshold layer but a ranked list of (layer, head) pairs ordered by their f-propagation contribution, and your intervention budget determines how far down that list you need to go to achieve near-complete suppression.

Head-wise value vector zeroing is indeed more parameter-efficient than layer-wise residual patching when L* is a distributed set of (layer, head) pairs, because you're cutting f-propagation at its transport mechanism rather than mopping it up after it has already spread — but "zeroing" is too blunt; the correct operation is projecting each implicated head's value vectors onto the orthogonal complement of f̂, preserving everything the head computes except its f-carrying component, analogous to the rank-1 weight editing in Meng et al.'s ROME (2023) but applied to attention value matrices rather than MLP weights. The stability question is the sharper issue, and the honest answer is that probe-trained f̂ vectors are likely to be delimiter-style-sensitive in their surface coordinates but stable in their functional direction: Todd et al. (2023, "Function Vectors in Large Language Models") showed that task vectors extracted from ICL prompts transfer across superficially different prompt formats — different delimiters, spacing, capitalization — because the underlying feature is "this token marks a demonstration transition" not "this token is literally '\n\n'", and a well-trained linear probe on diverse delimiter styles should recover the format-invariant direction. The practical test for stability is to train f̂ on prompts using one delimiter style (e.g. "Input:/Output:") and measure intervention effectiveness on held-out styles (e.g. "Q:/A:" or pure newline separation) — if cosine similarity between the delimiter-specific and delimiter-agnostic f̂ estimates exceeds ~0.85, the intervention will transfer; below that, you need a multi-style probe or a SAE latent that aggregates across formats. The failure mode that overfitting produces is specific and diagnosable: the intervention will over-suppress on trained delimiter styles (removing not just f but correlated task-relevant features that co-occur with those specific tokens) while under-suppressing on novel styles, producing an asymmetric accuracy profile that reveals the probe's format-dependence. McDougall et al. (2023) on copy-suppression heads showed that individual attention heads can have highly generalizable functional roles that transfer across token-surface variation, which is the mechanistic reason to be cautiously optimistic that the head-wise intervention will generalize — but this was demonstrated for syntactic/copying functions, and whether ICL-saturation features have the same format-invariant geometry is an open empirical question.
